title: Grades 3–5 Practice Test — Form A
tier: Classroom practice; not an ACCESS tier
overview: Four-domain classroom practice in listening, reading, speaking, and writing. Work at your own pace. Item difficulty, scoring, timing, and routing are not equivalent to ACCESS.

sections.title: Listening: A Class Trip to the Farm
sections.directions: You will hear a teacher or a visitor talk. Press play to listen. You can listen again if you need to. Then answer each question. Choose the best answer.

items.title: What to Wear
items.prompt: What should students wear to the farm?
items.scriptTitle: Getting Ready for the Farm Trip
script: Good morning, class. Tomorrow we are going on a trip to Green Hill Farm. The bus will leave at nine o'clock, so please come to school on time.
Wear old sneakers, because the paths at the farm are muddy. Bring a water bottle and a jacket. You do not need to bring lunch. The farm will give us a picnic lunch.
At the farm, we will visit three places. First, we will see the chickens in the barn. Next, we will pick apples in the orchard. Last, we will help plant pumpkin seeds in the garden.
items.correct: Correct. Ms. Okafor says to wear old sneakers because the paths are muddy.
items.support: The teacher tells what to wear and then says why.

items.title: The Farm Tour
items.prompt: Look at the picture of the farm. Which place does Farmer Amara talk about first?

picture.alt: A farm with a big red barn and chickens in front of it. Apple trees with red apples grow behind the barn. A vegetable garden with rows of small plants is next to a blue pond, and a farmer waves hello.

script: Welcome to Green Hill Farm! My name is Farmer Amara. This big red building is our barn. Inside, we keep twelve chickens. Every morning, I collect their eggs in a basket.
Behind the barn is our apple orchard. The apples are ready in the fall. When an apple is ready, it comes off the branch with a gentle twist. Please do not pull hard, or you can hurt the tree.

Our garden is next to the pond. Today you will plant pumpkin seeds. Make a small hole with your finger, drop in one seed, and cover it with soil. Then give it a little water. In about one hundred days, you will have pumpkins!
items.correct: Correct. Farmer Amara starts the tour at the big red barn.
items.hint: Listen to the very beginning of the tour.
items.support: Find each place in the picture as you hear about it.
wida: Connect oral language to a visual

sections.title: Reading: How Bees Help Plants
sections.directions: Read the passage. Then answer the questions. You can look back at the passage, the picture, and the chart as many times as you want.

items.title: Look Closely
items.skill: Using a picture with a text
items.prompt: Look at the picture. What is stuck to the bee's legs?

picture.alt: A close-up picture of a fuzzy striped bee standing on a big pink flower. Clumps of yellow dust from the flower are stuck to the bee's back legs and body.

passage: Bees are busy insects. They fly from flower to flower all day long. Bees visit flowers to drink a sweet liquid called nectar.
Flowers also have a yellow powder called pollen. When a bee lands on a flower, pollen sticks to the tiny hairs on its body and legs.
Then the bee flies to another flower. Some of the pollen falls off onto the new flower. This is called pollination. Pollination helps the plant make seeds and fruit.
Many foods we eat need bees. Apples, cherries, and pumpkins all need pollination. Without bees, farmers would grow much less fruit.
You can help bees, too. Plant flowers in a garden or in a pot by a window. Do not spray poison on flowers, because it can hurt bees.
items.correct: Correct. The yellow powder on the bee's legs is pollen.
items.hint: Read paragraph 2. What is the yellow powder called?
items.support: Find the yellow color in the picture and in the text.

sections.title: Speaking: Our Neighborhood Park
sections.directions: Look at each picture. Read how the model student started. Plan your ideas, then say your answer out loud in full sentences. Use the word bank to help you.

items.title: Describe the Park
passage: A model student, Diego, started like this: "I see a girl. She is holding a trash bag."
Now it is your turn. Plan your ideas, then say your answer aloud in full sentences.
items.adminScript: Look at the picture of the park. What are the people doing to help the park? Take a moment to plan. Then say your answer aloud in full sentences.
items.prompt: Look at the picture of the park. What are the people doing to help the park?
items.responseLabel: Planning notes (then say your answer aloud)
sayFor: name at least three people or things
tell what each person is doing (-ing words)

models.A: A girl. Trash. A boy, recycling. A tree.
models.B: I see a girl picking up trash. A boy carries a recycling bin. Two kids plant a tree. A man waters the flowers.
models.C: In the picture, neighbors are cleaning up the park together. A girl is picking up a can and putting it in her trash bag, while a boy carries a blue recycling bin. Two children are planting a small tree, and a man is watering the flowers so they can grow.

items.correct: Strong answer (model): In the picture, neighbors are cleaning up the park together. A girl is picking up a can and putting it in her trash bag, while a boy carries a blue recycling bin. Two children are planting a small tree, and a man is watering the flowers so they can grow.
items.hint: Point to each person in the picture. Say what that person is doing.
items.support: Use the word bank and the sentence frames. Say your answer out loud. Listen to the models to hear how answers grow.

picture.alt: Neighbors clean up a park. A girl picks up a can and holds a trash bag. A boy carries a blue recycling bin. Two children plant a small tree, and a man waters flowers with a watering can. There is a bench and a yellow slide.

items.title: Tell the Kite Story
passage: A model student, Mei, started like this: "First, a girl and her grandpa went to the park."
Now it is your turn. Plan your ideas, then say your answer aloud in full sentences.
items.adminScript: Look at the three pictures. Tell the story. What happened first, next, and last? Take a moment to plan. Then say your answer aloud in full sentences.
items.prompt: Look at the three pictures. Tell the story. What happened first, next, and last?
items.responseLabel: Planning notes (then say your answer aloud)
sayFor: tell what happens in all three pictures

models.A: Girl. Kite. Tree. Sad. Grandpa get kite.
models.B: First, a girl flies a kite. Next, the kite is stuck in a tree. She is sad. Finally, her grandpa gets the kite with a rake.
models.C: First, a girl was flying her red kite in the park while her grandpa watched. Then a strong wind blew the kite into a tall tree, and the girl felt very sad. Finally, her grandpa used a long rake to pull the kite down, and she cheered because she could fly it again.

items.correct: Strong answer (model): First, a girl was flying her red kite in the park while her grandpa watched. Then a strong wind blew the kite into a tall tree, and the girl felt very sad. items.hint: Say one or two sentences for each picture. Start with first, next, and finally.

sections.title: Writing: Our School Garden
sections.directions: Read each task. Look at the picture if there is one. Plan your ideas, then write in complete sentences. Use the word bank and sentence frames. Check your writing when you finish.

items.title: Our School Garden Story
items.prompt: Look at the four pictures. Write a story about the students and their garden. Tell what happened first, next, then, and last. Write 4 to 6 sentences.
writeFor: one or more sentences for each picture
an ending that tells how the students felt

models.A: Kids dig. Put seeds. Water. Flowers grow.
models.B: First, two students dug in the soil. Next, they put seeds in the holes. Then they watered the seeds. Finally, tomatoes and a sunflower grew.
models.C: First, two students dug small holes in the soil with their shovels. Next, Rosa dropped seeds into each hole and covered them. Then Malik gave the seeds water with a watering can. Weeks later, tall tomato plants and a giant sunflower grew, and a bee came to visit. Rosa cheered because their hard work made the garden grow.

items.correct: Strong response (model): First, two students dug small holes in the soil with their shovels. Next, Rosa dropped seeds into each hole and covered them. Then Malik gave the seeds water with a watering can. Weeks later, tall tomato plants and a giant sunflower grew, and a bee came to visit. Rosa cheered because their hard work made the garden grow.
items.hint: Write about each picture in order. Give the students names.
items.support: Use the word bank and the sentence frames. Read your writing again when you finish and fix one thing.

picture.alt: Four pictures in order. 1: Two students dig in the soil with small shovels. 2: A student drops seeds into the holes. 3: A student waters the soil with a watering can. 4: Weeks later, tall tomato plants with red tomatoes and a sunflower have grown, a bee flies by, and the student cheers.

items.title: Should Every School Have a Garden?
items.prompt: Should every school have a garden? Write your opinion. Give two reasons. End with a closing sentence. Write 4 to 6 sentences.
items.responsePlaceholder: I think every school should / should not have a garden.
frames: I think every school should / should not have a garden.

models.A: Yes garden. Learn plants. Good food.
models.B: I think every school should have a garden. One reason is that students can learn about plants. Another reason is that they can grow food. That is why schools need gardens.
models.C: I think every school should have a garden. One reason is that students can learn science outside, like how bees help plants make fruit. Another reason is that a garden gives students fresh vegetables to taste and share. A garden also teaches us to work as a team. That is why every school needs a garden.

items.hint: Say yes or no first. Then give two reasons.
